passages.text: But the Heracles who killed the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth—the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind. Naked of every vice, it ranges throughout the world, visiting souls and bringing those it meets to sound judgment; I mean people resembling bold lions, cowardly deer, wild boars, or many-sided hydras. Likewise, all the other things Heracles is said to have accomplished as labors are riddles of intellectual virtue. For now, let what has been said suffice, for not even all of time will be enough to speak about each one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τοῦ πλούτου ἡγεμόνα καὶ φύλακα ὄφιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both roles attributed to the serpent and the genitive relation to wealth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ὁ γνήσιος as identifying the true Heracles and καὶ φιλόσοφος with νοῦς, with καί represented by “also.” A material alternative coordinates γνήσιος and φιλόσοφος as qualifications of νοῦς: “Heracles is the genuine and philosophical mind.” The main rendering is retained because the article in ὁ γνήσιος naturally permits an appositional identification of Heracles, while the surrounding allegory identifies the genuine Heracles with mind.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bringing those it meets to sound judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονίζω can mean making someone prudent, self-controlled, or sound-minded; this wording suits the philosophical context.
πολύτροπος can mean manifold, versatile, devious, or many-natured; “many-sided” preserves its breadth without choosing only the moral sense “wily.”
νοερός concerns mind or intellect, matching the passage’s allegory of the philosophical mind.

source_issues.source_quote: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
source_issues.issue: The attachment of ὁ γνήσιος and force of καί are interpretively ambiguous. The main rendering attaches “true” appositionally to Heracles and understands καί as “also,” but ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφος may instead jointly characterize νοῦς, yielding “Heracles is the genuine and philosophical mind.” This is an attachment ambiguity, not evidence of a defective source.

passages.text: Still, I wonder how those who concealed these things in oblique riddles and veiled them over with wicked myths are called intelligent and wise by you, when the things could have been disclosed clearly, reverently, and beneficially by the uncovered, straight way. As though driven on by an evil demon, they laid snares for almost all humanity. For either these are not riddles but true sins of the gods—in which case they ought not to have exposed the gods or, in the first place, set those sins before human beings for imitation—or the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods were told in riddling form. And the men you call wise sinned, Appion, because by covering solemn things with indecent myths they encouraged human beings to sin, and did this while insulting those whom they even believed to be gods.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s contrast between an unveiled direct route and oblique, concealing riddles.
ἐνεδρεύω evokes lying in ambush or entrapping, rather than merely misleading.
ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or censure; “exposed” fits the argument that their sins should not have been publicized.
Under negation, τὴν ἀρχήν idiomatically means “at all” or “in the first place,” not merely “at the beginning.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context contrasts actual divine sins with false mythic representations. A more formally literal alternative is “the things falsely done by the gods.”
σεμνός may mean solemn, venerable, august, or dignified; the contrast is with indecent myths.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
source_issues.issue: ψευδῶς may be heard as modifying the alleged performance itself (“falsely done”) or the presentation of the deeds as divine. The surrounding contrast between true sins and riddling falsehood supports “falsely presented as having been done.”

passages.text: Therefore regard such people not as wise men but as evil demons, for they put forward wicked storylines for noble deeds, so that those wishing to become imitators of their betters might emulate the actions of the so-called gods. When speaking on the previous day I did not conceal those actions: I mean patricides, murders of children, impious unions with mothers, daughters, and sisters, unseemly adulteries, male-male intercourse, and defiled acts unfit to name, besides ten thousand other unlawful unions of this kind. Still more impious are those who want these things to be regarded as true, so that they may do the like without shame. In this matter, if they had really wished to act reverently, they ought—as I just said—even if the gods had in fact committed the evils sung about them, out of honor for the gods to have covered the indecent things with myths of a more seemly kind, and not the reverse: as you claim, when good deeds had been performed by them, to wrap them in evil and indecent forms. Such forms, when allegorized, can be understood only with labor and scarcely at that; and whenever some people understand them, they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided, while they have utterly destroyed those who were led astray. Nevertheless, I approve those who allegorize them toward the more dignified sense, such as those who intimated in a riddle that practical wisdom sprang from the head of Zeus. But perhaps this is more plausible to me: once wicked men had won the reputation of gods, those outrages were dared.

lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόθεσις may denote a subject, underlying premise, or dramatic plot; “storylines” fits myths that clothe supposedly good deeds in wicked narratives.
The comparative can refer to those superior to the imitators, here especially the beings called gods.
The compound directly denotes sexual intercourse between males; the rendering avoids importing a broader modern identity category.
μιαρός marks pollution or defilement, while the rare ἀρρητουργία denotes the doing of things that are unspeakable or not to be named.

lexical_decisions.chosen: out of honor for the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative phrase expresses the honor owed or directed toward the gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκείνοις μὲν ἀντὶ τοῦ πολλοῦ μόχθου παρέσχον τὸ μὴ πλανηθῆναι, ἐξὸν μὴ μοχθῆσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided
lexical_decisions.rationale: The benefit is identified as not being led astray, while μέν sets up the contrast with those who were led astray; the Greek does not expressly make this their only benefit.
φρόνησις is prudent or practical understanding, while ἀναπηδάω supplies the vivid image of springing forth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had won the reputation of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποφέρομαι with δόξαν can mean carrying off, gaining, or winning a reputation.

source_issues.source_quote: ὧν ἀσεβέστεροι οἱ ταῦτα ἀληθῆ δοκεῖν εἶναι θέλοντες
source_issues.issue: The antecedent and force of comparative ὧν are not fully explicit. It may mean “more impious than these” or introduce a subgroup, “among whom the more impious are.” The main text uses the defensible contextual sense “still more impious” without forcing an antecedent.

source_issues.source_quote: τοὺς εἰς τὸ σεμνότερον ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτὰς
source_issues.issue: The feminine pronoun αὐτάς may refer back to the actions or accounts implicit in the argument; its precise antecedent is not explicit. The English “them” preserves that referential openness.

passages.text: But we do not find the poetic allegory concerning all the gods consistent. To take an immediate example, in the ordering of the universe the poets say at one time that nature became the originator of the whole creation, and at another that mind did. For they say that the first motion and mingling of the elements arose from nature, but that this was ordered by the providence of mind. Although they declare that the universe was fashioned by nature, because they cannot demonstrate this beyond objection on account of the artistry of creation, they also interweave the providence of mind, thinking themselves able to sweep along even those who are very discerning. But we say to them: If the world came into being from spontaneous nature, how has it acquired proportion and order? These can be brought about only by surpassing intelligence and can be comprehended by knowledge, which alone is capable of determining these things precisely. But if all things received their combination and ordering through intelligence—which necessarily cannot be otherwise—how could these things then possibly have happened to come into being spontaneously?

lexical_decisions.rationale: ποιητικός can mean poetic or belonging to poets; “the poets’ allegory” is a viable alternative, but the adjective is preserved directly.
The passage contrasts nature and mind as competing explanatory first principles; lowercase English avoids imposing personification beyond the context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of the artistry of creation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔντεχνος denotes what is artful, skillfully made, or governed by craft.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even those who are very discerning
lexical_decisions.rationale: σαφής applied to people can describe those who are clear-minded, perspicacious, or discerning, while πάνυ marks a high degree, represented by “very” rather than a superlative.
Here φρόνησις concerns the intelligence responsible for cosmic proportion and order, while μόνης restricts what can bring them about.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ ἐπιστήμης τῆς μόνης ταῦτα ἀκριβοῦν δυναμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: can be comprehended by knowledge, which alone is capable of determining these things precisely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second μόνης belongs to the attributive phrase describing knowledge as alone capable of precise determination; it does not directly restrict the passive verb “can be comprehended.”
The phrase can also be rendered “by chance” or “of itself”; “spontaneously” maintains the connection with ἐξ αὐτομάτου φύσεως earlier in the argument.

passages.text: Therefore, those who wished to allegorize divine matters in the more shameful direction—for example, that Metis was swallowed by Zeus—have fallen into perplexity. They do not understand that those who gave oblique accounts of nature concerning the gods have also abolished their very existence as gods, dissolving their forms by allegory into the substances of the world. It is more plausible, then, to say that the gods celebrated by them were certain evil magicians. Though wicked human beings, they assumed different forms by magic, broke up marriages, and ruined lives; yet to people of old, who did not know what magic even was, they seemed to be gods because of what they did. In city after city, both their deaths and their tombs are evident.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to allegorize ... in the more shameful direction
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative phrase describes the direction or resulting sense of the allegorical interpretation, not simply its method.
In the mythic example Μῆτις is the conventional name Metis, although the name itself also means counsel or cunning intelligence.
φυσιολογέω means discoursing or theorizing about nature, while πλαγίως marks the indirect or oblique manner.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ εἴδη αὐτῶν ... εἰς τὰς τοῦ κόσμου οὐσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: their forms ... into the substances of the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the philosophical contrast between the gods’ forms or identities and the cosmic substances into which allegory resolves them.
μάγος here denotes practitioners of magic; the following μαγείᾳ confirms that sense.
The middle or passive participle can mean transforming themselves or being transformed; the context presents magical changes of appearance.
μόρος can mean death, doom, or allotted fate; its pairing with tombs favors “deaths,” though “fates” remains possible.

source_issues.issue: The supplied, image-checked print has a raised point before περὶ. This verified editorial punctuation leaves περὶ θεῶν capable of being associated either with the oblique account of nature or more loosely with the following claim about abolishing the gods. The translation provisionally takes it with the participial phrase while retaining the supplied reading; the punctuation is not treated as an OCR defect.
